note: Attacker-controlled PoC file is read line by line from disk, so the file contents directly drive the harness input.
The first line must be a mode header; this determines which architecture/mode selector byte is placed into Data[0].
The header text is parsed into attacker-controlled architecture and mode strings, which select the target decoder configuration.
For the crafted PoC header, the harness encodes the chosen architecture/mode into the first byte of the fuzz input.
Subsequent hex bytes from the PoC are copied into the input buffer, forming the attacker-controlled instruction stream.
The assembled bytes are passed into the disassembly harness, propagating the attacker-controlled payload into Capstone.
The selector byte chooses the X86-64 platform, ensuring the payload is decoded in the vulnerable code path.
A Capstone handle is created for the selected architecture/mode, establishing the decoder state used by the sink.
The attacker-controlled instruction bytes are handed to the disassembler, which may produce decoded instructions and metadata.
Decoded instruction bytes are copied into the output instruction structure; this is part of the propagation of attacker-controlled data through the decoder.
If decoding falls into skipdata handling, raw attacker-controlled bytes are copied into the cached instruction record.
The harness dereferences the decoded instruction and its detail pointer, exercising the decoder-produced structures that originate from the attacker input.

The final memory-safety sink is the cleanup path over the decoded instruction array; if the crafted input triggers a decoder bug that corrupts allocation state or instruction metadata, this free path is where the crash manifests.
